lessons.title: ਅ, ਆ — two pieces met inside a word you already say
lessons.gloss: two pieces of Gurmukhi, met inside a word you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ਅ, ਆ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach them.

segments.text: The two letters a Punjabi word uses when it opens on a vowel and has no consonant to hang a mātrā on.
First, say the last things you learned once more, out loud and from memory:
ਅ.
aiṛā — a. The bare vowel carrier. On its own it is a; with a mātrā hung on it, it is whatever that mātrā says.
ਆ.
aiṛā + kannā — ā. The vowel carrier wearing the kannā you already know — so it is long ā, at the start of a word.
Now put them where you have already heard them:
ਅ alone is a; ਆ is the same carrier wearing the kannā you already know. ਆ + ਸ becomes ਆਸ (ās) ਆਸ — ās — hope.
You are not being asked to write any of this. You are being asked to recognise it the next time it goes past.

blocks.title: Writing: copy what you can see

segments.text: Keep ਅ, ਆ in front of you and do not cover any of them. Follow each shape once with a finger, then copy it once with a pencil, larger than it is printed. Say its sound as your hand stops.
This is observe-and-trace with the model visible. Nothing in these chapters asks you to write a Punjabi word from memory; that ladder starts later, and it starts from these same shapes.

lessons.title: ਇੱਕ, ਦੋ, ਤਿੰਨ, ਚਾਰ, ਪੰਜ — one to five
lessons.gloss: one to five — meeting the panj of Punjabi as an actual number

segments.text: Four of these are new. The fifth you have known since Chapter 5 — you just didn't know it was a number.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the five

segments.text: This is Gurmukhi, not Devanagari — a related but distinct script. It does have a top line like Devanagari's, so words hang from a bar in the same way.
Count to five in Punjabi. (Ikk, do, tinn, chār, panj.) What script is this? (Gurmukhi — related to Devanagari, and it has a top line too.) Next: the two small marks riding on ikk, tinn and panj.

lessons.title: ੱ and ੰ — two marks, and five as a number
lessons.gloss: the addak and the tippi, and panj as a number

segments.text: Count to five once more: ikk, do, tinn, chār, panj. Three of those words carry a small mark above them. Which? (Ikk, tinn and panj.)
And the script you are reading: what does Gurmukhi share with Devanagari across the top of each word? (The top line.)

blocks.title: What you've built: two marks that look alike

segments.text: Two marks worth telling apart, because they look similar and do different jobs:
ੱ — the addak, on ikk. It doubles the following consonant.
ੰ — the tippi, on tinn and panj. It marks a nasal.
(So tinn's double n is not the addak's doing — that word is spelled with a nasal mark, and the doubling is in the pronunciation.)

blocks.title: What you've built: ਪੰਜ as a number

segments.text: Chapter 5 took the name ਪੰਜਾਬੀ (panjābī) apart for you: Persian ਪੰਜ panj, "five," plus ਆਬ āb, "water" — the language of the five rivers.
You learned panj there as a piece of a place-name. Here it arrives as what it actually is: the number five, an ordinary word you will count with.
The next prerequisite-ordered lesson explains an important twist: Punjabi's numeral and the Persian word reached the same panj shape independently.

segments.instruction: the two marks — "addak doubles, tippi nasalises"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two marks — "**addak** doubles, **tippi** nasalises"]

segments.instruction: the Ch. 5 callback — "panj + āb = five rivers"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the Ch. 5 callback — "**panj** + **āb** = five rivers"]

segments.text: What do ੱ and ੰ each do? (Addak doubles the following consonant; tippi marks a nasal.) Chapter 5 told you panjābī means "of the five rivers." What has changed now? (Panj is a number you can count with, not just a piece of a name.) Next: learn why Punjabi and Persian both say panj.

lessons.title: Panj: the odd one out among its neighbours
lessons.gloss: why Punjabi five looks like Persian, not like its neighbours

segments.text: Say “five” in Punjabi. (Panj.) Where did Chapter 5 first show that shape? (Inside Persian panj + āb, “five waters.”)
In ਪੰਜ, which mark sits on top, and what does it do? (The tippi, ੰ: a nasal.) And the addak, the small crescent? (It doubles the next consonant.)

blocks.title: What you've built: the surprising family comparison

segments.text: The neighbours keep a -ch shape. Punjabi matches Persian -j, but the obvious borrowing story is wrong.

segments.instruction: the neighbours' -ch — Hindi pāṁch, Bengali and Gujarati pā̃ch
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the neighbours' *-ch* — Hindi *pāṁch*, Bengali and Gujarati *pā̃ch*]

segments.instruction: the language whose "five" matches Punjabi's — Persian panj
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the language whose "five" matches Punjabi's — Persian *panj*]

segments.text: Which neighbours keep a -ch in "five"? (Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati.) Which language says panj, exactly as Punjabi does? (Persian.) So did Punjabi borrow it? Next: the answer is no.
Which other language says panj, exactly as Punjabi does? (Persian.) Was Punjabi's number borrowed from it?

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — Punjabi's numeral is homegrown

segments.text: Punjabi panj is inherited from Sanskrit pañca. North-western Indo-Aryan regularly voiced a stop after a nasal, turning -ñc- into -nj-.
Punjabi panjāh “fifty” (from Sanskrit pañcāśat) makes the rule visible; Hindi pacās shows the same source changing differently.

segments.instruction: Punjabi's path and proof — Sanskrit pañca becomes post-nasal -nj-; panjāh / pacās
segments.source: [YOU SAY: Punjabi's path and proof — Sanskrit *pañca* → post-nasal *-nj-*; *panjāh / pacās*]

segments.text: Borrowed from Persian? (No: Punjabi panj inherits Sanskrit pañca.) What made -nj-? (A post-nasal stop voiced.) Evidence? (Panjāh / pacās.) Next: how Persian reached the same shape.

segments.prompt: Was Punjabi panj borrowed from Persian?

feedback.correct: Right: Punjabi panj inherits Sanskrit pañca; Persian reached a similar shape separately.
feedback.incorrect: No. Punjabi panj is inherited from Sanskrit pañca, not borrowed from Persian.

lessons.title: Persian reached panj separately
lessons.gloss: Persian reached panj on its own: convergence, not borrowing

segments.text: Punjabi's panj comes from which Sanskrit word? (Pañca.)

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — Persian reached the shape separately

segments.text: Persian independently voiced ancestral č to j: Iranian panč became panj. Two Indo-Iranian branches therefore reached the same shape separately:

utterances: branch: Punjabi. path: Sanskrit pañca becomes nasal-triggered -nj-.
branch: Persian. path: Iranian panč becomes voiced panj.

segments.text: This is convergence, not borrowing. The place-name Punjab is Persian; Punjabi's look-alike numeral is inherited from Sanskrit.
